item.title: Microsoft Research unveils Magnetar: Faster, language‑agnostic zero‑knowledge proofs
item.description:
Microsoft Research unveils Magnetar: Faster, language‑agnostic zero‑knowledge proofs

Magnetar is the newest zero‑knowledge proof system from Microsoft Research. It can prove the correct execution of programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster than earlier comparable systems, and its security relies only on standard hash functions.

🔍 Overview

  • Runs a workload and produces, together with the output, a short cryptographic proof that the program ran correctly.
  • The proof is small and can be checked in milliseconds by anyone, without rerunning the program, without trusting the prover, and without needing the input data.
  • Verification can be passed on to others who need the same assurance.

🧩 How it works

  • Zero‑knowledge proofs allow a prover to convince a verifier that a computation was performed correctly while revealing nothing about private inputs.
  • Magnetar’s processor description builds on the Phalanx idea of exploiting repetition in a processor’s instruction cycle to accelerate proof generation.
  • The system is instantiated with hash‑based cryptographic primitives, eliminating the need for a trusted setup and avoiding elliptic‑curve‑based constructions.

⚙️ Key details

  • Supported languages: Rust, Go, C.
  • Performance: 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems.
  • Proof size and verification: Proofs are short; verification takes milliseconds.
  • Security basis: Relies only on standard hash functions, not on elliptic curves.
  • Zero‑knowledge property: The proof reveals no information about inputs that should stay private.

📚 Background

  • Zero‑knowledge proofs were invented in the 1980s; the concept of proving program execution has been around nearly as long.
  • Early practical approaches were limited to small programs and required either a layered sum‑check protocol or elliptic‑curve cryptography with a trusted setup.
  • In 2019, the Spartan system returned to the sum‑check approach, supporting general‑purpose programs without a trusted setup and allowing different cryptographic building blocks.
  • Phalanx (2021) demonstrated how to use repeated processor steps to achieve an order‑of‑magnitude speed improvement over Spartan.
  • Magnetar is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero‑knowledge proofs practical.

🔐 Security & Quantum Considerations

  • Many prior proof systems rest on elliptic curves, which can be broken by sufficiently powerful quantum computers.
  • Microsoft’s Quantum Safe Program aims to move products and services to post‑quantum cryptography by 2029.
  • Post‑quantum proof systems exist but often rely on newer cryptographic functions that have not undergone decades of scrutiny.
  • Magnetar’s reliance on standard hash functions avoids the unproven assumptions of newer primitives.

#ZeroKnowledge #Cryptography #MicrosoftResearch #VerifiableComputing

Source: Magnetar brings faster, simpler, quantum-ready zero-knowledge proofs

item.title: Jennifer Neville Discusses AI Evaluation on Microsoft Research Podcast
item.description:
Jennifer Neville Discusses AI Evaluation on Microsoft Research Podcast

Jennifer Neville, a Partner Research Manager at Microsoft Research, discussed the role of evaluation in pushing AI performance and the surprising failures that emerge when models are tested beyond traditional benchmarks in a conversation with Principal Applied Scientist Chad Atalla on the Microsoft Research Podcast.

🔍 Overview

In this episode of the Microsoft Research Podcast, Chad Atalla interviews Jennifer Neville, a partner research manager at Microsoft Research and the Samuel D. Conte chair professor of computer science and statistics at Purdue. Neville’s research examines machine learning and AI for interactive domains and structured data, focusing on how training data affects AI system behaviors and alignment with user needs. The conversation explores evaluation’s role in pushing AI performance boundaries and the “surprising failures” that emerge when models are tested beyond traditional benchmarks.

🧩 Key Details

  • Neville’s career path was unconventional: she majored in math, then physics, dropped out of college, returned to study cognitive science, and finally chose computer science despite initially avoiding it because her father was in the field.
  • She discovered AI by happenstance and got into research through an honors program requirement, publishing a paper on statistical relational learning that hooked her on the field.
  • Neville has published over 130 papers with more than 10,000 citations and received honors including a National Science Foundation CAREER Award, a spot on IEEE’s “10 to Watch” in AI list, and best paper awards from the International Conference on Data Mining and the International Conference on Learning Representations.
  • The episode also covers practical guidance for working with current AI systems and why closely examining data matters when results defy expectations.

#MicrosoftResearch #AIEvaluation #MachineLearning #Podcast #JenniferNeville

Source: What AI gets wrong and what failure teaches us - Microsoft Research

item.title: Microsoft Research Introduces Quine Multimodal World Model for Biology
item.description:
Microsoft Research Introduces Quine Multimodal World Model for Biology

Microsoft Research has introduced Quine, a research effort to create a multimodal world model of biology and an interactive harness that connects models, scientific tools, literature, and researchers.

🔍 Overview

Quine is designed to work across various biological boundaries, reflecting a vision for a discovery system that evolves through scientific use. It consists of two primary components:

  • A world model of biology: A system capable of representing the state of a biological system, predicting how that state evolves in response to interventions, and reasoning over the consequences of those interventions multiple steps into the future.
  • An interactive harness: A system that connects the world model to orchestration and reasoning models, scientific tools, literature, and research teams.

🧩 How it works

The core world model learns shared representations across biological modalities and scales, including:

  • Sequence
  • Structure
  • Function
  • Cellular state
  • Imaging data

By training across these modalities jointly, Quine can use evidence from one modality to inform predictions in another, capturing relationships that might be lost when separate single-domain specialist models are used. This integration allows researchers to generate predictions across modalities and reason about the consequences of biological interventions before wet-lab testing.

⚙️ Key details

Microsoft Research has applied Quine in collaboration with researchers at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard to study pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Through this work, they have used the system to prioritize compounds predicted to drive therapeutic tumor-state shifts and validated several top-ranked candidates across multiple wet-lab assays.

Quine is experimental research technology intended only for research, not for clinical or medical use. Its outputs may be incomplete or inaccurate and require review by qualified researchers and appropriate scientific and experimental validation.

🚀 Availability

  • Quine Fellows program: A cohort of scientists will be given access to the system to accelerate their research and provide scientific feedback.
  • Future Access: As the technology matures, Microsoft expects to expand access through products such as Microsoft Discovery.

#MicrosoftResearch #Biology #WorldModels #Biotech #AI

Source: Introducing Quine: An AI research system designed for the complexity of biology

item.title: Microsoft researchers show sliding-window attention rivals linear-attention models
item.description:
Microsoft researchers show sliding-window attention rivals linear-attention models

Microsoft Applied Sciences researchers have published findings arguing that sliding-window attention (SWA) with attention sinks can match or outperform post-trained linear-attention models on both short- and long-context tasks, challenging a recent wave of retrofits aimed at extending context windows in large language models.

🔍 Overview

The research team — Alexia Jolicoeur-Martineau, Rhea Sanjay Sukthanker, Pashmina Cameron, and Emy Gervais — positions SWA as a simpler alternative that avoids the need for post-training modifications while delivering competitive performance and efficiency.

⚙️ Key details

  • Performance: SWA with attention sinks reportedly achieves 2-10x higher scores than post-trained linear-attention models on two long-context benchmarks:
    • Needle-in-a-Haystack
    • BABILong
  • Efficiency claims: The researchers state SWA:
    • Requires no post-training
    • Runs fast
    • Uses little memory
  • Target: The work directly challenges recent linear-attention retrofits designed for long-context LLMs

💡 Why it matters

The findings suggest that a well-tuned conventional attention mechanism may eliminate the need for more complex architectural overhauls. If the efficiency claims hold, SWA could offer practitioners a lower-complexity path to long-context capabilities without the engineering overhead of post-training linear-attention conversions.

#slidingwindowattention #LLM #longcontext #attentionmechanism #MicrosoftResearch #AIarchitecture
